part_title: Lambda Fundamentals and Serverless Application Patterns

scenes.title: More Tools for Building AI Applications
scenes.narration: Welcome to Module Six. Imagine a student building a small online bookstore with an AI assistant. A customer asks, 'Where is my order, and can you summarise what I bought?' The foundation model can write a friendly explanation, but where will the real order information come from? That's the problem this module solves. Picture the request travelling through a series of responsibilities. An API accepts the customer's message and checks who is calling. Application code retrieves the correct order records, then sends only the necessary details to the model. If the task needs several steps, a workflow coordinates them. If thousands of requests arrive at once, messaging can keep the front end responsive while workers catch up. These are the supporting tools around generative AI. As we learn each one, ask a simple question: what problem does this component remove from our application? By the end, you'll be able to follow a request from the customer all the way to a safe, useful AI response, rather than memorising AWS service names without understanding how they fit together.

scenes.title: AWS Lambda: Serverless Data Processing
scenes.narration: Let's make this concrete with a document arriving in an S3 bucket. Suppose a customer uploads a PDF invoice and wants the assistant to find it later. The upload event is the starting signal. A Lambda function receives information about the new object, reads it with the permissions granted to its execution role, checks its format and prepares the next processing step. The important detail is that Lambda doesn't sit there continuously asking, 'Is there a new file yet?' AWS invokes our code when the configured event occurs. Imagine one upload today and a hundred tomorrow; the service handles the execution environments subject to scaling limits. Now, what if the PDF takes a long time to extract or needs multiple AI calls? We shouldn't force a huge workflow into one function. Instead, Lambda can start a managed job or send a message for later processing. So here's the mental picture: the event tells Lambda when to work, the handler defines what to do, and another service can take over when the work needs more time. That separation is why serverless processing is useful.

scenes.title: What Is AWS Lambda?
scenes.narration: Now let's open the Lambda function itself and examine the pieces a developer must configure. First is the handler: this is the function your code exposes to receive the incoming event. Next is the runtime, such as Python or Node.js, which runs that code. Then comes the execution role, and this is easy to overlook. If our handler needs to read an invoice from S3, the role must allow that operation. If it also invokes Bedrock, it needs permission for the chosen model. Writing a model ID in the code doesn't magically grant access. We also choose memory and a timeout. These settings influence how much work one invocation can perform and how it behaves when an operation is slow. Imagine the function receives an upload event twice. If the handler creates two invoices or charges a customer twice, the architecture is broken even though both invocations succeeded technically. That's why we use a stable document or order identifier to make processing safe to repeat. Remember the distinction: an event starts the function, the runtime executes code, the role authorises AWS calls, and the handler implements the business action.

scenes.title: Example: Serverless Website
scenes.narration: Let's build the website a customer actually sees. The page design, images and JavaScript are static files that a browser can download, often through S3-backed hosting and a content delivery service. But when the customer presses 'Show my recent orders,' a static file cannot answer that request. The browser sends an HTTPS call to API Gateway. The gateway matches the route and invokes the Lambda backend. Lambda checks the customer identity, retrieves only that customer's records, then sends a structured response that the page displays. Follow the return journey as carefully as the request: database result to Lambda, Lambda response to API Gateway, then JSON back to the browser. Notice what is missing: we never had to manage a permanently running web server just to execute that little handler. Now add Bedrock. Lambda can pass the authorised order details to the model and ask for a short, natural-language summary. The model doesn't browse every customer's orders by itself. This is the security lesson hidden inside a simple website diagram: the API controls entry, backend logic enforces access, and the model helps explain the data.

scenes.title: Example: Order History Application
scenes.narration: Let's finish our bookstore example by following one order from purchase to history. The customer confirms an order, the application writes the order details to a database, and the customer later opens the order history page. A Lambda-backed API can query the correct records using the customer's authorised identity, format the result and return it quickly. But suppose we also need an email receipt, an audit record and an AI-friendly summary. Should the customer wait while all three happen? Usually not. We can keep the read and checkout path responsive, then let background events or queued messages trigger the additional work. Each worker can process its task and retry a temporary failure independently. Imagine the same order-created event arrives twice. A stable order ID lets the worker recognise that the receipt or summary has already been produced, avoiding duplicate side effects. Finally, the assistant retrieves this particular customer's records and generates a readable summary. The big idea is that 'serverless' isn't a single magic box. It's a collection of focused services: one accepts the request, another executes business logic, a database holds the facts, and asynchronous workers handle the work that doesn't have to block the user.
